Holomorphic function (f∈O(U))

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis Complex analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 8k Articles: 87
A complex-valued function f:U→C is holomorphic on an open set U when it has a complex derivative at every point of U. Requiring a derivative throughout a neighbourhood is much stronger than complex differentiability at a point. It forces locally convergent Taylor series and derivatives of every order, as follows from the Cauchy integral formula and Cauchy derivative formula.
To see the restriction in real coordinates, write z=x+iy and f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y). The real and imaginary increment quotients must agree, giving the Cauchy-Riemann equations
ux​=vy​,uy​=−vx​,f′=ux​+ivx​.
(1)
Conversely, if u,v have continuous partial derivatives on U and satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann equations there, then f is a holomorphic function. The equations at a lone point, without a differentiability hypothesis for the real coordinate map, are insufficient. Their role is to force the Jacobian matrix to have the special form
Df=(ux​vx​​uy​vy​​)=(pq​−qp​),f′=p+iq.
(2)
Such a matrix represents multiplication by a complex number; it has only two free real entries. [ref]
For f(z)=z2, u=x2−y2 and v=2xy, so ux​=vy​=2x and uy​=−vx​=−2y. Directly,
f(z0​+h)−f(z0​)=2z0​h+h2,f′(z0​)=2z0​.
(3)
At z0​=1+i, multiplication by 2+2i scales lengths by its modulus 22​ and rotates by its argument π/4. A horizontal increment h=0.01 gives the exact displacement 0.0201+0.02i; a vertical increment h=0.01i gives −0.0201+0.02i. The first-order predictions 0.02+0.02i and −0.02+0.02i are perpendicular, and the errors have modulus 10−4.
At every nonzero z0​, this local rotation and scaling makes z2 a local conformal map. At zero, the first-order map vanishes: reiθ becomes r2e2iθ, so the argument doubles and the origin is a critical point. Globally z and −z have the same square. Local preservation of angles therefore coexists with global folding, a useful warning when using holomorphic functions as coordinate changes.

Weakly holomorphic Banach-valued function (φ∘f holomorphic for every φ∈X′)

Words: 199 Articles: 1
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
A map from an open subset of C into a complex Banach space is weakly holomorphic when every composition with a bounded complex-linear functional is a scalar holomorphic function. Norm holomorphy requires its difference quotients to converge in the Banach norm. Weak holomorphy is initially a condition on scalar observations; the weak holomorphy implies norm holomorphy argument recovers an actual vector derivative. A closed target subspace containing values on a sequence with an interior accumulation point contains every value on the connected domain: annihilate the subspace, apply the scalar identity theorem, and use Hahn-Banach separation.

Weak holomorphy implies norm holomorphy

Words: 115
Weakly holomorphic Banach-valued function OurBigBook.com
For a weakly holomorphic Banach-valued function, choose a closed disk contained in its domain. Each continuous functional is bounded on the image of that disk by scalar continuity. The Uniform boundedness principle, applied to its evaluation functionals in the bidual, gives a common bound M on the norms of the image vectors. Cauchy's formula on the disk's boundary then bounds the scalar difference between difference quotients at increments h,k by a constant times M∥φ∥∣h−k∣, uniformly for sufficiently small increments. Explicitly the difference kernel is
(ζ−z)(ζ−z−h)(ζ−z−k)h−k​.
(4)
The Hahn-Banach theorem dual norm formula converts this into the same norm bound for the vector difference quotients. They are Cauchy, so completeness gives a norm derivative. This also explains why weak holomorphy suffices without a separately assumed norm-continuity hypothesis.

Holomorphic extension (F∣U​=f,F∈O(V),U⊆V)

Words: 39
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
A holomorphic function F on a larger open set V whose restriction to U is the original holomorphic function f. A removable singularity is a point across which such an extension exists. On a connected larger domain, a holomorphic extension is unique by the identity theorem, provided U is nonempty.

Holomorphic surjection from the unit disc onto the complex plane (F(z)=z2/(1−z)2)

Words: 84
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
The rational function F(z)=z2/(1−z)2 is holomorphic on the unit disc and maps it onto the entire complex plane. For any w∈C, choose a square root r with Rer≥0 and put z=r/(1+r). The identity ∣1+r∣2−∣r∣2=1+2Rer>0 gives ∣z∣<1, while F(z)=r2=w. It is not injective: the two choices r=±i give distinct points in the disc with image −1.
A holomorphic bijection in this direction is impossible: its inverse would be a bounded entire function, contradicting the Liouville theorem. Thus a surjection onto the complex plane can exist even when a conformal equivalence cannot.

Conjugate reflection of a holomorphic function (f∗(z)=f(z)​)

Words: 92
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
If f is holomorphic on an open set U, its conjugate reflection f∗ is holomorphic on U∗={z:z∈U}, with (f∗)′(z)=f′(z)​. The identity follows by conjugating the difference quotient with increment h; the two conjugations restore complex differentiability.
If U is invariant under complex conjugation and is connected, and f is real at a set of real points accumulating inside U, then f=f∗ by the identity theorem. In particular, an entire function real at every 1/n has this symmetry. This is a symmetry statement on an already defined domain; Schwarz reflection also constructs extensions across a boundary.

Complex differentiability (f′(z)=limh→0​(f(z+h)−f(z))/h)

Words: 246 Articles: 1
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
A complex-valued function is complex differentiable at z0​ if
f′(z0​)=limh→0h∈C∖{0}​​hf(z0​+h)−f(z0​)​
(5)
exists. The same limit must hold for every approach, including curved paths. Equivalently,
f(z0​+h)=f(z0​)+f′(z0​)h+o(∣h∣).
(6)
The error divided by ∣h∣ tends to zero. Thus the derivative is a single complex multiplier, not an arbitrary real linear map of the plane. If the real coordinate map is differentiable, complex differentiability is equivalent to its satisfying the Cauchy-Riemann equations at that point.
The simplest failure is complex conjugation, f(z)=z. At every z0​ its increment quotient is h/h. For real h=t=0 it is 1, while for h=it it is −1. More generally, h=teiθ gives e−2iθ. Although complex conjugation is a smooth real reflection and has every real directional derivative, these incompatible quotients rule out a complex derivative everywhere.
Agreement on two axes is necessary, but does not by itself establish a limit over the whole complex plane. The Cauchy-Riemann equations need the real differentiability condition above, or a sufficient regularity condition such as continuous partial derivatives near the point. There is a second distinction: f(z)=∣z∣2 has complex derivative zero at zero because its quotient there is h→0, but its Cauchy-Riemann equations fail at every nonzero point. It is complex differentiable at zero without being a holomorphic function on any neighbourhood of zero.

Complex differentiability at a point without holomorphy nearby (f(z)=z/(1+∣z∣))

Words: 51
Complex differentiability OurBigBook.com
At zero, [f(h)−f(0)]/h→1, so the complex derivative exists. At a nonzero point, write r=∣z∣. The Cauchy-Riemann equations for x/(1+r) and y/(1+r) force x2=y2 and xy=0, impossible when r>0. Hence the function is complex differentiable only at zero and is holomorphic on no nonempty open subset. A complex derivative at one point gives no neighborhood of complex differentiability.

Nevanlinna class (N(D)={f:supr<1​∫log+∣f(rξ)∣dm(ξ)<∞})

Words: 139 Articles: 2
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
The analytic Nevanlinna class consists of holomorphic functions on the unit disc with uniformly bounded means of their positive logarithmic modulus. Here m is normalized angular measure. A bounded holomorphic function belongs to this class, but the class also permits unbounded functions. It is the analytic version of bounded characteristic.

Bounded characteristic

Words: 96 Articles: 1
Nevanlinna class OurBigBook.com
A holomorphic function on the unit disc has bounded characteristic when supr<1​∫log+∣f(rξ)∣dm(ξ)<∞, where log+t=max(0,logt). Thus it belongs to the Nevanlinna class. A general meromorphic function requires the additional pole-counting term in its characteristic; the displayed analytic definition has no such term.

Quotient characterization of bounded characteristic (f=u/v,u,v∈H∞(D),v≡0)

Words: 59
Bounded characteristic OurBigBook.com
A meromorphic function on the unit disc has bounded characteristic if and only if it has this representation. Its pole Blaschke product B makes g=Bf analytic with bounded positive logarithmic means. The least harmonic majorant by expanding disk lifts gives H≥log+∣g∣. A harmonic conjugate gives an analytic A with ReA=H, so u=ge−A and v=Be−A are bounded. Conversely the Nevanlinna first main theorem bounds the characteristic of u/v by that of u and 1/v, hence by a constant.

Multiplicity of a zero (ordz0​​f)

Words: 52
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
A holomorphic function that is not identically zero has a zero of multiplicity m at z0​ if f(z)=(z−z0​)mh(z) for a holomorphic function h with h(z0​)=0. Its Taylor series identifies m as the first nonzero coefficient index. Logarithmic differentiation gives f′/f=m/(z−z0​)+h′/h, so the residue of f′/f is m. Counting zeros with zero multiplicity repeats that zero m times.

Periodic holomorphic descent through the exponential map

Words: 83
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
If a holomorphic function of w is periodic with period one, then F((logz)/(2πi)) is independent of the choice of a local logarithm: two choices differ by 2πik, hence their arguments differ by an integer. Consequently it defines a holomorphic function on the image of the original domain under w↦e2πiw, provided that domain is invariant under integer shifts. Local logarithms prove holomorphy across an arbitrary global branch cut. Singularities on an integer lattice all map to z=1.

Constant-modulus holomorphic function

Words: 57
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
A holomorphic function with constant modulus on a connected domain is constant. If h=u+iv and u2+v2=c2>0, differentiation and the Cauchy-Riemann equations give uux​+vvx​=0 and −uvx​+vux​=0. Their coefficient determinant is −c2, so ux​=vx​=0, and all first derivatives vanish. When c=0, the conclusion is immediate. Consequently two nonvanishing holomorphic functions with equal moduli differ by a single constant phase on a connected domain.

Banach-space-valued holomorphic function (F′(z)=limh→0​hF(z+h)−F(z)​)

Words: 190 Articles: 2
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
A map from an open subset of C to a complex Banach space is holomorphic when the displayed limit exists in the Banach-space norm at every point. A norm-convergent power series is holomorphic inside its radius of convergence: on every smaller disk the series of derivatives converges uniformly by the geometric coefficient bound, allowing differentiation term by term. Applying a continuous linear functional produces an ordinary scalar holomorphic function. Scalar Cauchy identities therefore imply the corresponding vector-integral identities when bounded linear functionals separate points, as they do by the Hahn-Banach theorem.

Spectral-radius maximum principle (r(f(z))≤supw∈∂K​r(f(w)))

Words: 51
Banach-space-valued holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
For a Banach algebra-valued holomorphic function, set pn​(w)=∥f(w)2n∥1/2n. These continuous functions decrease to the spectral radius by the spectral radius formula. If M=sup∂K​r(f(w)), the continuous functions max{pn​,M} on ∂K decrease to the continuous constant M. The Dini theorem gives uniform convergence. Apply the norm maximum principle for a Banach-space-valued holomorphic function to each power, and then let n→∞. This proof does not assume continuity of spectral radius.

Norm maximum principle for a Banach-space-valued holomorphic function (∥f(z)∥≤supw∈∂K​∥f(w)∥)

Words: 54
Banach-space-valued holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
For a compact set K in the domain, a norming bounded linear functional at f(z) reduces the assertion to the scalar maximum modulus principle. If z lies inside K, use its connected component of the interior; that component's boundary lies in ∂K. If z∈∂K, the inequality is immediate. No smoothness or connectedness assumption on K is required.

Prescribed zeros in a plane domain via Runge approximation

Words: 105
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
Every closed discrete subset of a plane domain is the zero set of a holomorphic function, with assigned finite positive multiplicities if desired. Exhaust the domain by relatively filled compact sets. For a prescribed point outside an earlier compact, choose a rational factor with that zero and its possible pole outside the domain in the same complementary component. A slit joining zero and pole allows a holomorphic logarithm near the earlier compact. Approximate that logarithm by Runge theorem and multiply the rational factor by the negative exponential of the approximant. The resulting factors tend to one with summable errors on each compact. Their infinite product has the prescribed zeros and no additional zeros.

Antiholomorphic function (∂z​f=0)

Words: 52
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
A complex-valued function is antiholomorphic when its complex conjugate is a holomorphic function. In one complex dimension it locally depends on z and satisfies ∂z​f=0. A nonconstant antiholomorphic map reverses the orientation induced by the complex coordinates. Thus complex conjugating a holomorphic sphere map reverses its topological degree while preserving its Dirichlet energy.

Holomorphic convex hull (KΩ​)

Words: 103
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
For compact K in a plane domain Ω, its holomorphic convex hull is
KΩ​={w∈Ω:∣f(w)∣≤supK​∣f∣ for every f∈O(Ω)}.
(7)
It is K together with the components of C∖K lying entirely in Ω. Inclusion of those components follows from the maximum modulus principle. For exclusion, suppose w lies in a complementary component meeting C∖Ω. Choose an allowed pole there. The open-and-closed resolvent argument in the proof of Runge theorem approximates (z−w)−1 uniformly on K by functions h holomorphic on Ω. Then 1−(z−w)h(z) has value one at w and arbitrarily small modulus on K, separating w from the hull. For Ω=C, this is the polynomial hull in one complex variable.

Blaschke product (B(z)=λzm∏n​ban​​(z))

Words: 580 Articles: 8
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
For zeros an​ in the unit disc satisfying ∑n​(1−∣an​∣)<∞, with m occurrences at zero, a Blaschke product is
B(z)=λzm∏an​=0​an​∣an​∣​1−an​​zan​−z​,∣λ∣=1.
(8)
For ∣z∣≤R<1 and a=0, the normalized factor ba​ satisfies ∣1−ba​(z)∣≤(1−∣a∣)(1+R)/(1−R). The product therefore converges locally uniformly; outside its prescribed zeros the logarithms of its tail factors converge absolutely, so it has no additional zeros. Every finite product has modulus at most one in the disc, and the limit does too. Since ∣ba​(w)∣ is pseudohyperbolic distance from w to a, its modulus can be estimated geometrically.

Blaschke product OurBigBook.com
A finite Blaschke product is holomorphic across the unit circle and has modulus one there. For a constant a with ∣a∣<1, Rouché's theorem makes B−a and B have the same number of interior zeros, counting multiplicity. Each factor contributes its prescribed zero; the poles are outside the closed disk.

Hyperbolic zero estimate for a Blaschke product (∣B(w)∣≤exp[−2∑n​e−ρ(w,an​)])

Words: 49
Blaschke product OurBigBook.com
Use curvature-minus-one Hyperbolic distance in the Poincare disc. Each Blaschke factor has modulus tanh(ρ(w,a)/2)=(1−t)/(1+t), with t=e−ρ(w,a). For 0≤t<1, differentiating shows log[(1+t)/(1−t)]≥2t. Sum this logarithmic inequality over the zero factors and pass to the Blaschke product by locally uniform convergence. At a prescribed zero, its modulus vanishes and the bound is immediate. All sums count multiplicities.

Vanishing absolute logarithmic mean characterization of Blaschke products (∫∣log∣f(rξ)∣∣dm→0⟺f is a Blaschke product)

Words: 74
Blaschke product OurBigBook.com
For a holomorphic function on the unit disc, this boundary condition characterizes Blaschke products, including unimodular constants. The nondecreasing radial means of the nonnegative subharmonic function log+∣f∣ must vanish, so ∣f∣≤1. In the Blaschke factorization of a bounded holomorphic function f=Bg, both logarithmic means tend to zero. The mean value property for harmonic functions applied to log∣g∣ gives ∣g(0)∣=1, and the maximum modulus principle makes g unimodular constant. The converse follows from the radial logarithmic mean of a Blaschke product. Omitting the outer absolute value changes the condition: ez has zero mean logarithmic modulus, but is not a Blaschke product.

Blaschke factorization of a bounded holomorphic function (f=Bg,∥g∥∞​≤∥f∥∞​)

Words: 77
Blaschke product OurBigBook.com
Every nonzero bounded holomorphic function on the unit disc has this factorization, with B the Blaschke product of its zeros and g zero-free and holomorphic. The Blaschke condition follows from Jensen's formula. Dividing by any finite partial zero product gives a holomorphic function; the maximum modulus principle and the finite product's boundary modulus one bound that quotient by ∥f∥∞​. Locally uniform convergence of the partial products gives the same bound for g, with removable extensions at their zeros. This factorization alone does not make g constant or a full inner-outer factorization.

Blaschke product OurBigBook.com
For B(z)=λzm∏n​ban​​(z) with nonzero zeros an​ counted with multiplicity, Jensen's formula gives the displayed identity. The negative logarithms of partial products increase, so the monotone convergence theorem permits termwise integration. The Blaschke condition implies ∑n​−log∣an​∣<∞, which dominates the absolute summands. The dominated convergence theorem therefore gives a limit of zero as r↑1. Since ∣B∣≤1, the mean of ∣log∣B∣∣ tends to zero as well.

Automorphy character of an orbit Blaschke product (B(Tz)=χ(T)B(z))

Words: 77
Blaschke product OurBigBook.com
Let a group G of Möbius transformations of the unit disk have an orbit satisfying the Blaschke condition, counted once per distinct orbit point. For its Blaschke product B, invariance of the pseudohyperbolic distance and permutation of the orbit give ∣B(Tz)∣=∣B(z)∣. The ratio B(Tz)/B(z) extends across its zeros and has modulus one, so the open mapping theorem makes it a constant χ(T). Composition gives a group homomorphism χ:G→{λ:∣λ∣=1}. It is essential to compare moduli of the products: two arbitrary bounded holomorphic functions with identical zeros need not have constant quotient.

Blaschke condition (∑n​(1−∣an​∣)<∞)

Words: 114 Articles: 1
Blaschke product OurBigBook.com
The Blaschke condition for a sequence in the unit disc is ∑n​(1−∣an​∣)<∞. It characterizes the zero sequences, counted with multiplicity, of nonzero bounded holomorphic functions. Sufficiency follows by constructing the Blaschke product. For necessity, Jensen's formula gives ∑∣an​∣<r​log(r/∣an​∣)≤log∥f∥∞​−log∣f(0)∣ when f(0)=0. Letting r↑1 and using −log∣a∣≥1−∣a∣ proves the condition. A finite zero at zero is factored out first. Equivalently, for the curvature-minus-one hyperbolic metric, ∑n​e−ρ(0,an​)<∞, since e−ρ(0,a)=(1−∣a∣)/(1+∣a∣).

Blaschke sequence (∑n​(1−∣an​∣)<∞)

Blaschke condition OurBigBook.com
A sequence in the unit disc, counted with multiplicity, is a Blaschke sequence when it satisfies the Blaschke condition. The zeros of every nonzero bounded holomorphic function form such a sequence: Jensen's formula bounds ∑∣an​∣<r​log(r/∣an​∣) uniformly as r↑1, and 1−∣a∣≤−log∣a∣ gives the assertion. There are only finitely many zeros at the origin, which can be factored out first.

Jensen's formula (log∣f(0)∣+∑∣aj​∣<R​log(R/∣aj​∣)=2π1​∫02π​log∣f(Reiθ)∣dθ)

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
Let R>0 and let f be a holomorphic function on an open neighbourhood of the closed disk {z:∣z∣≤R}. Assume f(0)=0 and that f has no zeros of a function on the boundary circle ∣z∣=R. List its interior zeros of a function as a1​,…,aN​, repeating each according to its multiplicity of a zero. With the natural logarithm, Jensen's formula states
2π1​∫02π​log∣f(Reiθ)∣dθ=log∣f(0)∣+∑j=1N​log∣aj​∣R​.
(9)
The empty sum is zero. This boundary-zero-free version is the holomorphic special case of the general identity in the source.[ref]
Every interior zero of a function makes a positive contribution; a zero nearer the centre contributes more. Consequently boundary growth relative to ∣f(0)∣ limits how many zeros of a function can lie well inside the disk. The Jensen zero-count bound makes this quantitative, while the integrated zero count retains the individual radial weights. The boundary statistic here is the circle log-mean of a holomorphic function; exponentiating gives a circle geometric mean of a holomorphic function.

Under the hypotheses of Jensen's formula, the circle log-mean is the angular average of the natural logarithm of the complex modulus. The factor 1/(2π) normalizes the integral to a mean. Gf​(R)=exp(2π1​∫02π​log∣f(Reiθ)∣dθ)=∣f(0)∣∏j=1N​∣aj​∣R​.

Jensen's formula OurBigBook.com
Divide f by its finitely many interior zero factors, with each factor repeated according to its multiplicity of a zero. The resulting holomorphic function g has no zeros of a function in the closed disk, so log∣g∣ is a harmonic function and its circle average is log∣g(0)∣ by the mean value property for harmonic functions. For each removed factor z−a, with 0<∣a∣<R, the circle average of log∣Reiθ−a∣ is logR: factor out Reiθ and apply the mean value property for harmonic functions to log∣1−(a/R)w∣ on a neighbourhood of the closed unit disk. Analytic continuation

Words: 2k Articles: 20
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
An analytic continuation extends a holomorphic function beyond its original domain without changing its existing values. Formally, if U⊂V are domains and f is holomorphic on U, a holomorphic function F on V with F∣U​=f is an analytic continuation. More locally, holomorphic functions on overlapping open sets continue one another when they agree on the overlap, allowing a chain of patches along a path. The identity theorem for holomorphic functions forces agreement throughout a connected overlap once they agree on a nonempty open set in it. It also makes an extension to a fixed connected domain unique. [ref]
The geometric series illustrates why a formula can reach farther than the power series that first represents it. For z=1, its partial sum is
SN​(z)=∑n=0N​zn=1−z1−zN+1​.
(20)
When ∣z∣<1, zN+1→0, so the series converges to f(z)=1/(1−z). The rational function F(z)=1/(1−z) is holomorphic on C∖{1} and agrees there with the sum on the unit disc. It therefore continues f to every point except its simple pole at 1. In particular,
f(1/2)=2,F(2)=−1,SN​(2)=2N+1−1⟶+∞.
(21)
Thus analytic continuation gives a value at 2 without making the original geometric series converge there. Its radius of convergence remains 1: on ∣z∣≥1 the terms zn do not even tend to zero.
The pole at 1 limits the original Taylor series, although most points of its convergence circle are regular for F. Recentring at −1 gives another genuinely convergent power series,
F(z)=2−(z+1)1​=21​∑n=0∞​(2z+1​)n,∣z+1∣<2.

At z=−3/2 this yields 21​∑n≥0​(−1/4)n=2/5, even though the original powers of −3/2 grow. This is the useful idea: overlapping local descriptions can represent one holomorphic function on a larger region.
Uniqueness on a connected overlap does not imply that every path leads to the same terminal germ of a holomorphic function. Continuing a complex logarithm around 0 changes its value by 2πi, giving monodromy; the return patch can carry a different branch of a multivalued function. If two patches have a disconnected overlap, agreement on one component imposes no agreement on the others. [ref] Continuation using the rational function 1/(1−z) is single-valued: any path avoiding 1 gives the same terminal germ of a holomorphic function, even if it winds around the pole.

Monodromy theorem

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Analytic continuation OurBigBook.com
The monodromy theorem says that, when analytic continuation exists throughout a domain, its ambiguity depends on homotopy. Let D⊂C be a domain, a∈D, and ga​ a germ of a holomorphic function at a. Assume ga​ admits analytic continuation along every continuous path in D starting at a. Two such paths ending at b give the same terminal germ of a holomorphic function if they are homotopic with endpoints fixed in D. [ref]
Here a homotopy with endpoints fixed is a continuous map H:[0,1]2→D satisfying
H(0,t)=γ0​(t),H(1,t)=γ1​(t),H(s,0)=a,H(s,1)=b.
(24)
Every intermediate path must stay in D. Equality means agreement on a neighbourhood of b, rather than merely equal values at b. [ref]
The identity theorem provides local rigidity; the monodromy theorem shows precisely how topology controls the remaining global freedom. Deforming a route without crossing a forbidden point cannot change the resulting germ of a holomorphic function. Thus a complicated analytic continuation calculation can be replaced by one on a simpler homotopic route. Distinct homotopy classes can still give the same continuation: a rational function on its domain already gives a single-valued answer along every route, even around a pole.

If a holomorphic representative G near 1 continued f, then the identity theorem would extend (1−z)G(z)=1 to that neighbourhood. Substituting z=1 would give 0=1. Thus the pole prevents the existence hypothesis, although C is a simply connected domain. The analytic continuation article explains why the same rational function does continue throughout C∖{1}.
Existence at an endpoint by some route is also weaker than existence along every path from the base point. Along the real segment from 1 towards 0, a holomorphic square root of z tends to 0, yet cannot continue holomorphically through 0: a local representative G would satisfy G2=z by the identity theorem, and differentiating at 0 would give 2G(0)G′(0)=1 with G(0)=0. A finite limiting value therefore does not remove a branch point. More severe obstructions appear at a natural boundary of a holomorphic function.

For a covering map p:X→Y and base point y, the path lifting theorem lifts each based loop from each point of the fibre p−1(y). Its endpoint defines a permutation of that fibre; path reversal gives the inverse. The homotopy lifting theorem for a covering map makes the permutation depend only on the based homotopy class. These permutations form the monodromy group, the image of the fundamental group action

(28)
The image is independent of the convention for composing routes; one may reverse the loop classes to obtain a left group action when route multiplication means following the first route and then the second.
For p(w)=w2 on the punctured plane, the fibre over 1 is {1,−1}, and a once-around based loop exchanges its two points. The monodromy group has two elements: only the parity of the winding number matters. For the covering map p(w)=ew from the complex plane to the punctured plane, the fibre over 1 is 2πiZ, and a positive turn acts by 2πik↦2πi(k+1). Its monodromy group is an infinite cyclic group. These are the geometric versions of logarithm and square-root continuation along different paths: the base point returns, while its lifted endpoint can move to another sheet.

The degree-four rational map F(z)=z2+z−2 has branch values −2,2,∞. Away from their inverse images, the transformations
z↦−z,z↦z−1
(29)
are commuting deck involutions. They generate a Klein four-group acting transitively on each fibre
{z,−z,z−1,−z−1}.
(30)
Consequently the monodromy group is V4​, acting by the identity and the three double transpositions.

If a parameter-dependent contour integral has a moving pole, deforming the integration contour continuously so that the pole never crosses it preserves a holomorphic branch. Returning the contour to its original path after crossing a pole adds or subtracts the corresponding residue contribution.

If the interval integral instead uses (t2−1)z=e−iπz(1−t2)z, the corresponding identity includes the extra factor eiπz. Omitting this phase changes the value, rather than merely the locations of the meromorphic continuation's poles.

Entire function (f:C→C holomorphic everywhere)

Words: 2k Articles: 15
Holomorphic function OurBigBook.com
An entire function is a holomorphic function whose domain of a function is the whole complex plane. Its derivative exists at every z∈C. Every polynomial, the complex exponential function ez, the product zez, and the complex sine function sinz are entire functions. The Taylor series of an entire function about any finite centre converges throughout the complex plane.
The complex exponential function is a particularly revealing entire function. Writing z=x+iy, Euler's formula gives
ex+iy=ex(cosy+isiny),∣ex+iy∣=ex>0.
(32)
Thus the complex exponential function never takes the value zero. Conversely, for any w=0, choose an argument θ of w. All its preimages under the complex exponential function are
zk​=ln∣w∣+i(θ+2πk),k∈Z.
(33)
Here ln∣w∣ is the real natural logarithm, and k ranges over the integers. Substitution gives ezk​=∣w∣eiθ=w; equality of moduli and arguments shows these are all the solutions. The complex exponential function therefore has image exactly C∖{0}, with infinitely many preimages for each nonzero value.
In the pictured vertical strip −1≤x≤1, the real part sets the modulus between e−1 and e, while the imaginary part sets the argument modulo 2π. The two drawn bands each make one full turn around the same annulus; their corresponding points differ by 2πi and have identical images. Allowing all real x gives every positive modulus, so the whole complex plane covers every nonzero output.
An entire function has exceptionally strong global constraints. The Liouville theorem says that a bounded function which is also an entire function must be a constant function. Accordingly, the nonconstant entire functions above are unbounded somewhere in the complex plane, even when their restrictions to the real axis are bounded: the complex sine function satisfies sin(iy)=isinhy, growing through the hyperbolic sine. The Little Picard theorem adds a different constraint: an unbounded nonconstant entire function still cannot leave two distinct complex values out of its image. These results make entire functions useful when global bounds or restrictions on the image can establish rigidity without solving for the function explicitly.
In the opening of his 1880 memoir, Émile Picard credits Karl Weierstrass with the terminology of entire functions and describes them by everywhere-convergent power series. [ref]

Injective entire functions are affine (g(z)=az+b,a=0)

Words: 62
Entire function OurBigBook.com
An injective holomorphic function cannot have an essential singularity: Casorati-Weierstrass theorem would give values from a small punctured neighbourhood inside the open image of a disjoint neighbourhood, contradicting injectivity. Apply this at infinity to an injective entire function. A removable singularity there would make the function constant by Liouville's theorem. A pole makes it a polynomial by the Cauchy coefficient formula; its derivative has no zero, so the fundamental theorem of algebra forces degree one.

Exponential polynomial (F(z)=∑j​Pj​(z)eλj​z)

Words: 84
Entire function OurBigBook.com
An exponential polynomial is a finite sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials. For distinct exponents, its terms are linearly independent over the polynomial ring: to isolate one term, apply the product of operators (D−λj​)degPj​+1 for all the other terms. On the remaining polynomial each operator becomes D+λ0​−λj​, which is injective because its nonzero constant preserves the leading coefficient. A nonzero exponential polynomial is an entire function of exponential type. Its maximum-modulus logarithm is O(R+logR), and Jensen's formula gives at most O(R) zeros, counted with multiplicity, in a disk of radius R.

Order of an entire function (ρf​=limsupR→∞​loglogMf​(R)/logR)

Words: 56
Entire function OurBigBook.com
For a nonconstant entire function, put Mf​(R)=max∣s∣≤R​∣f(s)∣. Its order measures the exponent in its exponential growth. Bounds logMf​(R)=O(RlogR) imply order at most one; a matching lower bound along the positive real axis proves order exactly one. This distinction is stronger than mere entire analyticity and controls the genus in Hadamard factorization.

An entire function is of exponential type if constants A,B>0 give the displayed bound everywhere. A genus-zero canonical product with ∑n​∣an​∣−1<∞ obeys ∣∏n​(1−z/an​)∣≤exp(∣z∣∑n​∣an​∣−1), since 1+u≤eu for u≥0.

Weierstrass factorization theorem (F(z)=zmeh(z)∏j​Epj​​(z/aj​)nj​)

Words: 381 Articles: 5
Entire function OurBigBook.com
A nonzero entire function can be described by its discrete zero locations and multiplicities, a product of Weierstrass elementary factors and a zero-free exponential factor. Conversely, consistent prescribed multiplicities at distinct points escaping every compact subset can be realized by choosing factor orders large enough for infinite product convergence from logarithmic tails. Repeated locations with incompatible exact multiplicities are not admissible data, and a finite accumulation of distinct zeros is excluded by the identity theorem.

Canonical product (∏n​Epn​​(z/an​))

Words: 207 Articles: 2
Weierstrass factorization theorem OurBigBook.com
A canonical product builds a prescribed discrete zero set from Weierstrass elementary factors. Choose the orders pn​ so that the logarithms of tail factors converge uniformly on each compact subset. Infinite product convergence from logarithmic tails then gives an entire function with exactly those zeros, counted with the prescribed multiplicities. When ∑n​∣an​∣−1<∞, factors of order zero suffice.
Canonical product construction for zeros escaping to the disk boundary (F(z)=zm∏n≥1​En​(z/an​))
Words: 61
Canonical product OurBigBook.com
For nonzero prescribed zeros an​ with ∣an​∣→1, the Weierstrass elementary factors of increasing order give the displayed holomorphic function on the unit disc; m handles finitely many zeros at zero. On any compact disc, eventually ∣z/an​∣≤q<1, and ∣logEn​(z/an​)∣≤qn+1/[(n+1)(1−q)]. The infinite product convergence from logarithmic tails gives a nonvanishing tail. The finite initial factors supply exactly the prescribed zeros and multiplicities. No Blaschke condition is required unless boundedness is imposed.

Ea,w,K​(z)=z−wz−a​exp(∑k=1K​k1​(z−wa−w​)k)
(34)
has exactly one zero in D, a simple zero at a. For ∣z−w∣>2δ(a) its zero-free holomorphic logarithm satisfies
∣logEa,w,K​(z)∣≤∑k>K​k2−k​≤K+12−K​.
(35)
Thus products of such factors can realize prescribed zeros approaching the boundary. If the zero has multiplicity m, choose the logarithmic error smaller by a factor m before taking the mth power. On a compact subset of D, eventual uniform summability of these logarithms gives a nonvanishing product tail and a holomorphic function with precisely the requested zeros.

Hadamard factorization theorem

Words: 52
Weierstrass factorization theorem OurBigBook.com
An entire function of finite order factors as its canonical zero product times the exponential of a polynomial. For order at most one and nonzero value at zero, it has the form f(z)=f(0)eBz∏j​(1−z/aj​)ez/aj​. Genus-one factors converge when ∑j​∣aj​∣−2<∞. A zero-free function of this order is therefore the exponential of an affine polynomial.

Weierstrass factorization theorem OurBigBook.com
If two nonzero entire functions have identical zeros and orders, their quotient extends to a nowhere-zero entire function. Its logarithmic derivative has a primitive on the simply connected plane, producing a holomorphic logarithm h and the displayed relation. Any two choices differ by one constant integer multiple of 2πi. On a multiply connected domain the logarithm can fail to exist globally.

Pointwise vanishing derivative criterion for a polynomial

Words: 44
Entire function OurBigBook.com
Suppose that for every z∈C, at least one derivative f(n)(z) of an entire function vanishes. The closed sets En​={z:f(n)(z)=0} cover C. By the Baire category theorem, some EN​ has nonempty interior. The identity theorem gives f(N)=0 everywhere, so f is a polynomial of degree below N.

Picard theorem

Words: 959 Articles: 3
Entire function OurBigBook.com
The Picard theorem has two forms concerning the image of a holomorphic function. The Little Picard theorem permits at most one omitted value for a nonconstant entire function. The Great Picard theorem is local: near an isolated essential singularity, every complex value except possibly one occurs infinitely often. The complex exponential function ez and the function e1/z show that the possible exception is necessary.
Émile Picard presented the research in 1879 and published proofs in his 1880 memoir. Its opening footnote lists communications to the Académie des Sciences on 28 April, 19 May, and 20 October 1879; sections 3 and 15 contain the global and local results respectively. [ref]

Omitted value (w∈/f(D))

Words: 58
Picard theorem OurBigBook.com
An omitted value of a function f:D→Y is a point w∈Y outside its image: the equation f(z)=w has no solution in D. Both D and Y matter. The complex exponential function on the complex plane has one omitted value in C, namely zero, and two omitted values when regarded as a map into the Riemann sphere, namely zero and infinity. Restricting D can create additional omitted values.

Little Picard theorem (#(C∖f(C))≤1)

Words: 800 Articles: 1
Picard theorem OurBigBook.com
Every nonconstant entire function takes every complex value with at most one exception. Equivalently, its image is either C or C∖{a} for one complex number a. The hypothesis of being nonconstant matters: a constant function has only one value. The Little Picard theorem guarantees existence of preimages, without requiring infinitely many preimages for each attained value. [ref]
For a nonconstant polynomial p, the fundamental theorem of algebra applied to p(z)−w supplies a preimage for every w∈C. The complex exponential function has precisely one omitted value, zero, as the explicit formula for its preimages shows. In contrast, the complex sine function has no omitted value. To solve sinz=w, set u=eiz and rearrange to the quadratic equation
u2−2iwu−1=0.
(36)
Its roots have product −1, so they are nonzero. Every such root has a preimage under the complex exponential function, giving a solution for z. Adding 2πk supplies further solutions by the periodicity of the complex sine.
The force of the Little Picard theorem is that it applies to every nonconstant entire function, without an explicit formula. The Liouville theorem already gives a dense image of a nonconstant entire function, but a dense subset could still leave out many individual points. The Little Picard theorem limits these missing points to one. In particular, establishing two omitted values proves that an entire function is constant.
For a nonconstant meromorphic function on the complex plane, the corresponding bound is two omitted values in the Riemann sphere C∪{∞}, where poles take the value infinity. [ref] For example,
m(z)=1−ez1​
(37)
omits zero and one, and has poles at 2πik for k∈Z. Every other finite value w is attained by solving ez=1−1/w. For an entire function, infinity is already an omitted value in the Riemann sphere, leaving at most one additional finite omitted value.
Proof outline: use the version of Montel's theorem for two fixed finite omitted values. [ref] It makes the rescaled holomorphic functions gn​(ζ)=f(a+nζ) a normal family on the unit disc. The fixed value gn​(0)=f(a) gives pointwise anchoring of a holomorphic normal family, hence a subsequence with a finite holomorphic function as its locally uniform convergence limit. The Cauchy integral formula bounds its derivatives at zero, whereas gn′​(0)=nf′(a). Consequently f′(a)=0; arbitrary a makes f constant.
Great Picard theorem (#{z:0<∣z−a∣<r, f(z)=w}=∞)
Words: 480
Little Picard theorem OurBigBook.com
Let f be a holomorphic function on 0<∣z−a∣<R, and suppose a is an isolated essential singularity. There is a set E⊆C with at most one element such that, for every w∈/E and every 0<r<R, the equation f(z)=w has infinitely many distinct solutions with 0<∣z−a∣<r. Thus each nonexceptional value has preimages accumulating at a in every punctured neighbourhood. The same possible exception works for all these neighbourhoods; it need not be a completely omitted value, since it could be attained only finitely often near a. [ref]
The basic example is f(z)=e1/z at a=0. It is a holomorphic function for z=0, and its Laurent series
e1/z=∑n=0∞​n!z−n​
(38)
has infinitely many nonzero negative-power terms, making zero an essential singularity. Its sole omitted value is zero. For the value one, its preimages are exactly
zk​=2πik1​=−2πki​,k∈Z∖{0}.
(39)
They satisfy e1/zk​=1 and ∣zk​∣=1/(2π∣k∣)→0. For any r>0, every integer k with ∣k∣>1/(2πr) therefore supplies a distinct solution inside 0<∣z∣<r.
The diagram displays only finitely many preimages; the formula and its limit, rather than the finite picture, establish that infinitely many occur in every punctured neighbourhood. More generally, for any w=0, choose an argument θ of w. All its preimages are
zk​=ln∣w∣+i(θ+2πk)1​,k∈Z,
(40)
with any zero denominator excluded. Such an exclusion occurs only for w=1, with exactly one excluded integer k for the chosen argument. The remaining preimages are distinct and tend to zero as ∣k∣→∞.
The isolated essential singularity hypothesis is crucial. The function f(z)=z−1 has a pole at zero; on 0<∣z∣<r its image is only {w:∣w∣>1/r}. It omits every value in the closed disc ∣w∣≤1/r, and each attained value has just one preimage. A pole therefore has entirely different local behaviour from an essential singularity.
The Casorati-Weierstrass theorem says that the image near an essential singularity is a dense subset of the complex plane. The Great Picard theorem replaces arbitrary approximation by exact attainment, and then repeats that attainment infinitely often. This is useful when a local restriction on the image can rule out an essential singularity and reduce the possibilities to a pole or a removable singularity. For a meromorphic function viewed as a holomorphic map into the Riemann sphere, the corresponding statement has at most two exceptional sphere values, including infinity in the count; it applies when the map has an isolated essential singularity, even if poles accumulate there. Picard's 1880 memoir proves the local result in section 15, treating the cases with and without accumulating poles separately. [ref]
The Great Picard theorem also explains the Little Picard theorem. For a nonconstant polynomial, every value is attained by the fundamental theorem of algebra. For an entire function which is not a polynomial, the function g(ζ)=f(1/ζ) has an essential singularity at zero: a removable singularity would force f to be constant by the Liouville theorem, and a pole would force f to be a polynomial. Applying the Great Picard theorem to g leaves at most one finite omitted value for f.
